processing: An unoxidised green tea rolled into tight, fine, round strands. The local method is said to have taken shape in the 1920s, when growers drew on techniques from Huang Da Cha and Gua Pian.
harvest_season: Spring, as with other Xinyang maojian; the earliest tender pickings are the most valued.
appearance_dry: Tight, fine, round and straight strands with visible downy tips.
taste_profile: A high, clear aroma with a strong note of roast chestnut; the body is mellow and rich, with a sweet, cooling finish.

brewing.notes: Fine downy strands release quickly, so keep the first steep short. Add the leaf after the water in a glass if you want to see it sink.

vintage_note: Sold as a current-year spring tea, as is usual for Xinyang greens, and best within about a year. Pickings before the Qingming and Guyu festivals usually cost more. Cheyun Mountain is a small named area inside the Xinyang Maojian region, so the mountain name on the label deserves a question or two.
description:
Cheyunshan Maojian comes from Cheyun Mountain in Xinyang, in the Tongbai range on the Henan and Hubei border. It is one of the 'five clouds, two pools and one stockade' named as the core places of Xinyang Maojian, so think of it as a specific address inside a famous tea.

The leaf is rolled into tight, fine, straight strands with the downy tips left showing. There is no oxidation, so what you taste is the fresh leaf and the heat of the drying.

The thing to look for is the chestnut: a clear, high aroma with a strong note of roast chestnut, over a mellow, full body with a sweet and cooling finish. The liquor is a clean tender yellow. Water too hot or a long first steep will turn that into bitterness quite quickly.

Because the name carries a premium, ask for the harvest date and the village, and compare it with an ordinary Xinyang Maojian. A good lot should be even and fresh-smelling. Keep it sealed and cool, and drink it within the year.
history: Tea is said to have been grown on the mountain before the Qing, with stronger growth under the Guangxu reign. The maojian method itself is dated to the 1920s, when local growers adapted techniques from other teas. Some tea references also say the tea was shown at the 1915 Panama exposition.
